newsitem.title: JORDAN: Germany says Israel should reconsider settlements.
newsitem.headline: Germany says Israel should reconsider settlements.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Wednesday that Israel should reconsider a decision to build Jewish settlements in Arab East Jerusalem which sparked international condemnation.

Kinkel, who met King Hussein on Tuesday night at the start of a trip to Jordan, Israel and Palestinian-ruled Gaza, said he would convey to Israel's government the king's "deep concern" over plans to build 6,500 Jewish homes around the holy city.

"My feeling is that the Israeli government should reflect again," Kinkel, speaking through an interpreter, told a news conference. "I cherish the hope, and will make it very clear when I visit Israel, that Israel will reconsider this decision."

He said he supported a European Union statement last week which deplored the Israeli settlement plan at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel, as contravening international law and forming an obstacle to peace.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has said building on the tree-topped Jerusalem hill would fuel mistrust and Arab states have denounced it as a violation of the peace accord with Palestinians.

Kinkel also implicitly criticised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's decision to shut down four Palestinian offices in East Jerusalem. Israel says the offices handle Palestinian Authority affairs in violation of the same 1993 accord.
"Given the present difficult situation I think we should avoid decisions which foster mistrust," Kinkel said.
But he said he would relay to the Israeli government Germany's and Jordan's "determination to react in a calm and balanced manner".
"The peace process is without alternative," he said.

Kinkel also met on Wednesday EU Middle East envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos, who plans to visit Damascus soon in an attempt to revive peace talks between Syria and Israel, which have been on hold for a year.

He said Germany felt there were signs of movement between Syria and Israel, but because of his country's delicate relations with the Jewish state it was not seeking the political mediation between Arabs and Israel attempted by the United States, France, or the European Union.

"Because of what happened in the past, Germany should take a less prominent position," he said, alluding to Germany's role in carrying out the Holocaust killings of millions of Jews during World War Two.
Instead Europe's economic powerhouse would give financial assistance to projects which could give help revive Arab-Israeli cooperation.

Kinkel, who was accompanied by 15 businessmen and trade and finance officials, said Germany was ready to help fund a planned joint water project between Israel and Jordan, if the two countries could agree on its implementation.
"Water will play a very decisive part in the agenda of foreign policy (in the region)" he said. "Scarcity of water makes the issue central."
